messages.subject: RE: density plots on same data produce different results?
parts:
If you use geom_density instead of geom_freqpoly, you will get the same result with qplot(….., geom="density"…, )

 

So, try this:

depth_dist + geom_density(aes(colour = cut), binwidth = 0.1)

 

Hope this helps,

Kaori

 

From: ggp...@googlegroups.com [mailto:ggp...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of tce...@gmail.com
Sent: Thursday, April 04, 2013 10:25 AM
To: ggp...@googlegroups.com
Subject: density plots on same data produce different results?

 

Hi - 

 

I am very much enjoying getting my head around ggplot2() and have been working through the examples in Hadley's book ggplot2.

 

Today I came across something odd when making densities two different ways.

 

First via geom_freqpoly

depth_dist <- ggplot(data=diamonds, aes(x=depth)) + xlim(55,68)

depth_dist + geom_freqpoly(aes(y = ..density.., colour = cut), binwidth = 0.1)

which produces this:

 

 

Then via qplot's geom="density", called like this:

qplot(x=depth, data=diamonds, geom="density", xlim=c(55, 68), fill=cut, alpha = I(0.2))

which produces this:

 

 

My question is: why is the yellow region (cut = good) higher in the first plot than the second?   Indeed, in the first plot cut=fair peaks notably higher than the peak for cut=ideal. But in the second plot the opposite is true.  I think this is consequential because one might draw different conclusions looking at the two plots.

 

On the geom_freq_poly plot I tried adjusting bins to a bunch of different levels

And on the qplot one I tried including an `adjust=` parameter with a bunch of different values. Using smaller values does make the densities rougher but they seem to take on an increasingly random, 'fuzzy' quality rather than track the actual contours of the data more closely (like finer bin width might).

But even with these tweaks I can not get the peaks to be the same on the two plots. 

 

If I am being dense (no pun intended) and am somehow not looking at the same data or the same variables please do let me know - always a possibility. If not, I am curious to know which one would be considered more "correct". I realize both are doing different forms of bucketing, smoothing, etc. But I would have thought something like the relative height of the peaks might be preserved across the different methods.

Great - Thanks all. 

Makes sense that the density plot is generally smoother than the histogram. I was just surprised by the peak, though in retrospect I see that this is really an "optical" difference rather than saying something fundamentally different about the two distributions relative to each other. 

Best regards, TC
